requirements:
Implement a deterministic round-robin CPU scheduler in Rust as a SINGLE source file that compiles with rustc --edition 2024, using std only. Output ONLY the Rust source code inside ```rust fences.

The entire public API is below. Every listed type, field, and function must be public; every listed type must derive Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq. Do not add required arguments or change field types. Time intervals are half-open [start,end). There is no textual input/output protocol.

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Job { pub id: u32, pub ticks: u32 }
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Run { pub id: u32, pub start: u64, pub end: u64, pub finished: bool }
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Schedule { pub runs: Vec<Run>, pub completion: Vec<(u32, u64)>, pub end: u64 }
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Error { Quantum, SwitchCost, TooManyJobs, DuplicateId { index: usize }, Ticks { index: usize } }
pub fn schedule(jobs: &[Job], quantum: u32, switch_cost: u32) -> Result<Schedule, Error>;
```

R1. The signature and value types above are exact. All calls are independent and leave jobs unchanged. Job IDs may be any u32, including 0 and u32::MAX.

R2. Validation completes before simulation. Return only the first error according to R3 through R7, even for empty input.

R3. First, quantum must be in 1..=1000; otherwise return Error::Quantum.

R4. Second, switch_cost must be in 0..=1000; otherwise return Error::SwitchCost.

R5. Third, at most 64 jobs are allowed; otherwise return Error::TooManyJobs.

R6. Next inspect jobs in input index order. At each index first check whether its id equals any earlier id; if so return Error::DuplicateId { index }.

R7. At that same index, after the duplicate check, ticks must be in 0..=1000; otherwise return Error::Ticks { index }. An earlier row error wins over any later row error.

R8. Begin at time 0 with one FIFO queue containing all job indices in input order.

R9. Remove the queue head for each dispatch. A positive-work dispatch runs for min(quantum, remaining ticks), without interruption.

R10. After a positive-work dispatch, append an unfinished job to the queue tail; remove a finished job permanently.

R11. A zero-tick job completes at the time it is removed from the head, even if earlier jobs have already consumed time. It produces no Run and no time increment.

R12. Track the id of the last positive-work dispatch. Zero-tick jobs neither replace nor clear that id.

R13. Immediately before a positive-work dispatch, if a last id exists and differs from the selected id, advance time by switch_cost. The first positive-work dispatch is free.

R14. Consecutive positive-work dispatches of the same id incur no cost, even if zero-tick jobs were removed between them.

R15. A dispatch cost is a gap between Runs. It never produces a Run and is never charged after the final job completes.

R16. Append exactly one Run for each positive-work dispatch, in chronological order. Never merge adjacent Runs, even for the same id.

R17. Run.start is the time after any dispatch cost; Run.end is start plus consumed ticks. Run.finished is true exactly when this dispatch consumes the job's final ticks, including an exact quantum boundary.

R18. Record each completion at the current time after its last Run, or at removal for a zero-tick job.

R19. Schedule.completion contains exactly one (id, completion_time) per input job, in input order, regardless of completion order.

R20. Schedule.end is the time when the queue becomes empty, including all charged gaps. For no jobs or only zero-tick jobs it is 0.

R21. An empty input with valid parameters returns empty runs and completion and end 0. Arithmetic is exact u64 with no wrapping; the specified bounds make every result fit.
